text: The interpretive history of the *bnei elohim* ("sons of God") in Genesis 6 is among the strangest in the reception history of the Bible. The Book of Enoch, an ancient Jewish work preserved most fully in Ethiopic versions and read as scripture by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, elaborated a tradition of fallen angels, the Watchers, who descended to corrupt humanity through forbidden teaching and miscegenation. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 may presuppose this fallen-angel reading of the passage. Augustine, in *City of God*, rejected the angelic interpretation and favored the Sethite reading: the sons of God are the godly line of Seth, and the daughters of men are the line of Cain. Readers have also compared Genesis 6 with ancient Near Eastern traditions in which kings and other powerful men claimed descent from gods. The flood narrative introduced by Genesis 6 belongs to a broader Mesopotamian flood tradition, preserved most fully in the *Atrahasis* epic and in tablet XI of the *Epic of Gilgamesh*, the Utnapishtim narrative, where close parallels to the biblical flood story appear. The Hebrew word for the vessel Noah builds is *tevah* ("ark," "chest"), and outside the Noah story Scripture uses *tevah* only for the basket in which the infant Moses is set adrift on the Nile.
